answer.evidence: The sign is a flat, front-facing board. Rows 1-4 are a light header strip with a red label slot inside it, so it reads as a face-on header panel. The gray row 4 and the dark row 5 under it look like a frame edge and outline. The bottom (rows 30-31) repeats the same gray-then-dark pattern, which makes the top and bottom a symmetric front frame rather than a foreshortened horizontal surface. The width profile is 10, 12, then a constant 14, with no ellipse or widening-and-narrowing plane. The red panel (rows 6-29) with cream characters is a vertical face with no receding top or side face. At most a 1-2 row rim could be a top, so this is a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a narrow vertical sign. It has 9 visible tones per tile, which is above bus-shelter-a (6) and below kiosk-a (12) and vending-a (20). Near-flat coverage is 0%, so it has no 5x5 flat fills. The dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, matching the references, so the outline is a tinted dark red-brown and not a black sticker line. The body shows about 4 steps: a dark red panel, a lighter red bevel or border, a cream border or text, and a deep outline. The Hangul text is hand-pixelled and carries some highlight variation. It is a bit simpler than kiosk-a and vending-a, which are busier machines. For a thin single-purpose sign it sits within the range of the shipped references and would not look flatter or more sticker-like beside them.

The width is a constant 14 from row 3 downward, with no ellipse and no receding side face. There is no horizontal top surface of 3+ rows with its own front-edge line and eave shadow, so this is a front elevation.

The frame outline leans toward the material colour, and the measured near-neutral share of dark edge pixels is 0%, so it is not a black sticker line. It shows about 4 steps on the red ramp (frame, dark, mid, highlight edge) plus the light lettering and a post or base. It has 9 visible tones per tile, which is above bus-shelter-a (6), a little below kiosk-a (12) and well below vending-a (20). Near-flat coverage is 0%, against 9% for bus-shelter-a, so there are no large flat fills; the lettering and bevel break up the face. It is a thin, simple sign, so it is judged by eye rather than by density alone. Next to the references it does not look flatter or more sticker-like than bus-shelter-a, and it is comparable to kiosk-a in craft. Row 4 is a distinct grey-blue line (L=132) under the white rows (L=235), and row 5 is a dark navy line (L=17) that works as the eave shadow. That meets evidence (a). The red slot in the band is ambiguous, because it could also be a face-on label. The maroon panel (rows 6-28) with its cream lettering is a vertical front face of about 25 rows, closed off by a grey base at rows 29-31. No side face is drawn. Because the band is borderline, the main top surface is measured at 4 rows.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin, sparse vertical sign. It has 9 visible tones per tile, which is above bus-shelter-a (6) and below kiosk-a (12) and vending-a (20). Near-flat coverage is 0%, against 9% for bus-shelter-a, so there are no large flat fills. The dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, and by eye the outline is a dark red-brown that leans toward the red body rather than a black sticker line. The red body has about 4 steps: dark rim, mid red, lighter inset border and shadow side, with white lettering on top. That is slightly less than the richer references, but it is richer than the accepted bus-shelter-a. A careful artist would accept it beside these references without it looking flatter or more sticker-like.
